name: Voltage Regulator

claims.claim_text: Regulator type can be read off a board by eye. A small three-terminal package surrounded by capacitors could be either kind, but an inductor sitting next to it settles the question: that combination means a switching converter rather than a linear one.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's a switching because there's an inductor right next to it. That's a dead giveaway
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Olive-a The World

claims.claim_text: Recognising circuit blocks by their physical layout is learned rather than innate. The shapes and arrangements mean nothing at first and become obvious with enough exposure, which is why experienced engineers can identify a function from a photograph.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's definitely not intuitive at first
claims.episode_title: Olive-a The World

claims.claim_text: The trap in a cheaply priced 32-bit microcontroller is the core supply. A part needing a separate low core voltage cannot run directly from your existing rail, so an extra regulator joins the design and the system cost stops resembling the part price.
claims.quote_verbatim: You've got to add an extra regulator for that
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jack Ganssle - Embedded Elchee Epexegesis

claims.claim_text: The economics underneath that are simple: you pay per square area of silicon, so with all else equal an 8-bit part remains cheaper than a 32-bit one regardless of how the headline prices compare.
claims.quote_verbatim: you pay per square area of silicon
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jack Ganssle - Embedded Elchee Epexegesis

claims.claim_text: Some parts remove the problem entirely with an on-chip core regulator. The die runs internally at 1.5 or 1.8 volts while the package is powered from an ordinary rail, and the designer's only obligation is a bypass capacitor.
claims.quote_verbatim: the built-in voltage regulator takes care of it
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Biarchy Birthday Bavardage

claims.claim_text: Process geometry keeps pushing core voltages down, to around 0.9 volts, while input and output pins stay near 3.3. Whether a part integrates its own core regulator is therefore one of the first selection questions rather than a detail.
claims.quote_verbatim: 0.9 volts cores these days
claims.episode_title: 3D Printed Shark Jumps - Edifying Edison's Energy

claims.claim_text: The cumulative effect on a modern board is substantial: five separate regulators can be needed just to run one processor, each with its own passives and its own board area.
claims.quote_verbatim: you need five regulators just to do the, just to run a bloody call these days
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Magical Fire Bags

claims.claim_text: Removing a required rail simplifies a board disproportionately. When one FPGA family dropped its 2.5 volt requirement, the design could run from USB five volts with a couple of regulators and nothing else.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can bring in the 5 volts from the USB, put a couple of regulators on there
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Dave Vandenbout - Xceptional XESS Xenagogue

claims.claim_text: That rail had existed only for auxiliary configuration circuitry, which made it pure overhead: a whole regulator and its passives supporting something incidental to the part's actual function.
claims.quote_verbatim: it was all auxiliary stuff, so it was kind of a waste to have that out there
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Dave Vandenbout - Xceptional XESS Xenagogue

claims.claim_text: Some processors need a supply that varies with clock speed, in one case between 1.2 and 1.35 volts. That requirement cannot be met by sharing an existing rail and forces a dedicated adjustable regulator.
claims.quote_verbatim: the processor needs a variable supply between 1.2 and 1.35
claims.episode_title: An Interview with David Kronstein (Tesla500)

claims.claim_text: Local regulation is what lets an awkward part live on a board whose supply does not suit it. Putting a small regulator next to a device that needs an unusual rail means the board can be fed from whatever is available.
claims.quote_verbatim: you might even put a local voltage regulator on there
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Transistor Types and Where To Get Electronic Gear

claims.claim_text: A classic stability failure comes from reading only half the capacitor specification. A datasheet calling for a minimum output capacitance may also assume a minimum equivalent series resistance, so substituting a modern ceramic of the correct value gives too little resistance and the regulator oscillates.
claims.quote_verbatim: oops, it oscillates, because it's actually too low in ESR
claims.episode_title: Capacitors, Simulation and Closures - Deonerated Design Dealmaking

claims.claim_text: Shutdown and quiescent current describe different states and get confused. In shutdown the regulator is off and the output is not regulated at all, while quiescent current is what the part draws while holding the output in regulation with no load, so the rail is ready the instant the load wakes up.
claims.quote_verbatim: the regulator is still keeping the output in regulation, although your load is not drawing any current
claims.speaker: Andrea Longobardi
claims.episode_title: Low Power Connected Devices with Andrea Longobardi

claims.claim_text: Wake-up time is specified alongside that current, typically requiring the rail to be back in full regulation within microseconds to milliseconds, because a low-power state is only useful if leaving it is fast.
claims.quote_verbatim: respond within like, what, like a hundred microseconds
claims.episode_title: Low Power Connected Devices with Andrea Longobardi

claims.claim_text: Switching converters intended to sit near a radio are designed around the spectrum rather than only around efficiency: pushing the switching frequency to two megahertz puts it above the AM band, and spreading the switching frequency reduces the peak emissions, both of which exist to make the customer's compliance testing easier.
claims.quote_verbatim: So they were out of the AM band
claims.speaker: Andrea Longobardi
claims.episode_title: Low Power Connected Devices with Andrea Longobardi

claims.claim_text: A processor power regulator is a complete mixed-signal system inside one package, carrying sensitive analog lines, digital buses and power transistors within a few millimetres square. Treating it as a component understates what is happening inside it.
claims.quote_verbatim: as like a whole mixed signal PCB, just in one package
claims.episode_title: Switching Converter Engineering with Carmen Parisi

claims.claim_text: The distance between a simple three-terminal linear part and modern processor power delivery is enormous despite both being called voltage regulators, a difference of specification and performance comparable to two vehicles that are both technically cars.
claims.quote_verbatim: both are cars technically and very different in terms of specs
claims.episode_title: Switching Converter Engineering with Carmen Parisi

claims.claim_text: There is an architecture role between applications and circuit design: specifying what the control loop needs in terms of error amplifier gain and bandwidth, then negotiating against what the designers can deliver on schedule and judging whether the regulation specification still holds with what comes back.
claims.quote_verbatim: we need to have an error amplifier gain of, you know, XDB and Y bandwidth
claims.episode_title: Switching Converter Engineering with Carmen Parisi

claims.claim_text: A widespread misunderstanding of the adjustable three-terminal regulator: the reference is a fixed voltage between the output and the adjust pin, not a feedback node held at that voltage relative to ground. Tying adjust to output through a series resistor therefore turns the part into a current source, with the reference divided by that resistor setting the current.
claims.quote_verbatim: the 1.25 reference voltage drop divided by the series resistor gives you your output current
claims.episode_title: Bubblegum Tap Shoes

claims.claim_text: A crude but effective production fix for a regulator that needs a minimum load to stay in regulation is a power resistor in parallel with the output, guaranteeing the part always draws its minimum current whatever the real load is doing.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you just assume that it always pulls at least 100 milliamps
claims.episode_title: An Interview With Bil Herd - Zany Z80 Zygology

claims.claim_text: The crudest approach still works when you need a rail immediately: a linear regulator from the parts drawer and a stack of batteries produces five volts. The cost is that the entire input-to-output difference is dissipated as heat.
claims.quote_verbatim: you're burning all that power
claims.episode_title: Prototyping, Machining & Accelerators- Mugwumps Mulling Milling

claims.claim_text: An improvisation worth knowing: with no optocoupler available in the field, a five volt regulator fed from a 24 volt supply provided the level conversion, because the current involved was low enough and a couple of extra passives handled the switching. The temporary fix stayed in service for about two years.
claims.quote_verbatim: can we not just use a five volt regulator?
claims.speaker: Ronald Sousa
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ronald Sousa of Hash Define Electronics

claims.claim_text: A systematic field failure caused purely by margin: a five volt regulator rated to 21 volts input running from a 24 volt supply. Many of them failed, and the fix was simply fitting a properly rated part. Check the absolute maximum input against the actual supply rather than the nominal one.
claims.quote_verbatim: only rated to 21 volts DC input. And the power supply is 24
claims.speaker: Ben Heck
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ben Heck(endorn)

claims.claim_text: Regulators frequently act as sacrificial protection. When something upstream goes wrong they die and shield the circuitry behind them, which is why a repair on old equipment can mean replacing several of them before the instrument comes back.
claims.quote_verbatim: regulators don't do a bad job at actually protecting the circuitry that's behind there
claims.episode_title: Specialized and/or Open Source Test Gear and Dev Boards - Vacation Videography Vorboten

claims.claim_text: Older instruments distribute regulation widely rather than centrally, taking plus and minus 18 volt rails down to plus and minus 15 for the analog sections and eight volts down to five for the digital, which can put twenty regulators on a single board.
claims.quote_verbatim: there are 20 regulators on board these days
claims.episode_title: Specialized and/or Open Source Test Gear and Dev Boards - Vacation Videography Vorboten

claims.claim_text: The single most common kit assembly failure is a three-pin regulator fitted backwards, and it arrives reported as a design defect after the builder has checked everything else. The part is identifiable at a glance on a returned board.
claims.quote_verbatim: the 78 L05 voltage regulator was in backwards in the TO92 package
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: EcoWoke and Going Broke

claims.claim_text: The design response to that failure is clearer silkscreen marking. Orientation is genuinely not obvious to a beginner looking at a three-pin package, so the marking is doing real work rather than decorating the board.
claims.quote_verbatim: markings are really important
claims.episode_title: EcoWoke and Going Broke

claims.claim_text: A support lesson that follows: troubleshooting by email does not work, because every measurement is a round trip of hours. Either the person has an instrument and knows how to use it interactively, or the exchange goes nowhere.
claims.quote_verbatim: you cannot troubleshoot by email
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Vecordious Vacation Variorum

claims.claim_text: The discipline when someone reports your hardware is broken is to resist the reflex that it must be the firmware or the other party's fault, and to go and check all the supply voltages first. The reflex is strong and usually wrong.
claims.quote_verbatim: take a deep breath, and then go check all of the voltages
claims.episode_title: Funding New/Manufacturing Old Projects - Radical Robotic Requisition

claims.claim_text: Powering a precision measurement circuit directly from batteries lets its offset drift as the cells discharge, which shows up as a slowly changing result rather than an obvious fault. Adding a regulator is what makes the measurement stable over the life of the battery.
claims.quote_verbatim: as the batteries, like, drop, the offset voltage will change
claims.episode_title: Hamvention, Arduino and Intel - Burdensome Background Battology

claims.claim_text: A defect in one part can end a whole product. Adding external Schottky diodes in parallel with a regulator brought the drop from 0.6 to 0.3 volts and back inside specification, but the unresolvable question was how to prove that a one-in-a-hundred failure rate did not remain.
claims.quote_verbatim: what happens if one in 100 fail?
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Project Management, Lasers & Robots - Staunch Specialty Sanctanimity

claims.claim_text: Parametric search does not cover pin function, so there is no way to filter regulators by whether they have a shutdown pin. Vendors name and implement those pins differently, which leaves manual reading of datasheets as the only method.
claims.quote_verbatim: they don't classify it by what pins they have
claims.episode_title: Radiation Chips & Old Package Types - Technocratic Toilet Troubleshooting

claims.claim_text: An unwanted control pin is a small liability rather than a free feature: it has to be tied off correctly, usually through a resistor, and is one more thing to get wrong. Designers actively filter them out when the function is not needed.
claims.quote_verbatim: I didn't want an extra pin to have to mess up
claims.episode_title: Radiation Chips & Old Package Types - Technocratic Toilet Troubleshooting

claims.claim_text: Fixed-output regulators in the common voltages cost around a cent, which is why one appears in almost every design. At that price the decision is which one rather than whether to have one.
claims.quote_verbatim: they're one cent
claims.episode_title: PITA Package

claims.claim_text: Supply risk concentrates here despite the low cost. Regulator packages are often specialised enough that an unavailable part is not footprint-compatible with anything else, so a shortage forces a redesign rather than a substitution.
claims.quote_verbatim: these are like, you know, super specialized footprints
claims.episode_title: Living Through Chipageddon

claims.claim_text: Distributing power across a network of interconnected boards turns the supply into a resistor grid problem that is tedious to analyse. Putting a regulator on each device absorbs about a volt of drop and removes the need to do the analysis at all.
claims.quote_verbatim: we put regulators on board each, each device
claims.speaker: Zach Fredin
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Zach Fredin

claims.claim_text: Specifying generously at the supply removes a class of user problems: an eight amp five volt regulator on a USB hub lets every downstream port deliver two amps, which adds cost but means anything plugged in will power up.
claims.quote_verbatim: eight amp five volt regulator on board
claims.speaker: Chris Osterwood
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Chris Osterwood

claims.claim_text: A wrong resistor value in a regulator's feedback network produces a plausible but incorrect output rather than an obvious failure. The board comes up, the rail is simply not what it should be, and nothing points at the cause.
claims.quote_verbatim: the 40k was in the feedback network of a different regulator
claims.episode_title: Assembly Chat

claims.claim_text: A supply can regulate on voltage and current at the same time by running two control loops in parallel and letting whichever demands the smaller pulse width take control. That arrangement is what handles a load whose resistance changes during operation, such as a plating bath being loaded and unloaded.
claims.quote_verbatim: whoever says it wants the smallest wave, PBM wins
claims.speaker: Fredrik Kensander
claims.episode_title: High Current Power Supplies with Fredrik Kensander

claims.claim_text: A product built to an extreme price may omit regulation entirely, which is visible in use: the display fades whenever the device starts a high-current operation, because the supply sags and nothing is holding the rail up.
claims.quote_verbatim: they haven't even got a voltage regulator in there
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Engineering Optimization
